rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and Methods and Results; a two-season (2014-2015) field experiment at the CER experimental farm near Bologna, Italy, in which a Cosmos probe was installed over a mixed-crop area and its soil moisture compared with soil cores, in-situ sensors and profile probes (Table IV, Figures 7-17).
rows.notes: The study reports only that Cosmos soil moisture agrees with cores, sensors and profile probes for the top 0-50/60 cm (RMSE 0.029-0.067, overall 0.039) and that a soil moisture deficit can be computed from it and colour-coded against FAO stress thresholds (Figures 2b, 18). It does not implement Cosmos-based irrigation scheduling, nor measure irrigation water applied, water savings or water-use efficiency; the statement that Cosmos 'could be made operational' for deciding when and how much to irrigate is a proposal, not a tested result. This is a precondition (accurate area-based soil moisture/SMD measurement) of the claimed water-conservation effect, so upstream is set to true. Note the authors state limitations of the measurement itself (no access tubes beyond 100 m, biomass correction relying on SALTMED-simulated dry matter), but these are not limitations of a result on water conservation, which the study does not report.

notes: Full text appears complete. The study is a sensor validation/feasibility paper for cosmic-ray neutron sensing (Cosmos) in irrigated fields; it does not test irrigation scheduling outcomes or water-use efficiency.
